name: LifeAt
tagline: Virtual study and work spaces: scenic video backdrops, lofi audio, a Pomodoro timer, and a to-do list in one browser tab.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The functional core here is a video loop, an audio player, a countdown timer, and a checklist, all of which an agent can assemble in an afternoon. Nothing about the value depends on other users being present or on data only LifeAt has. What LifeAt actually sells is taste: a big library of licensed scenes and music, sensible defaults, and an interface that does not feel like a hobby project. If you already have a couple of ambient videos or YouTube live streams you like, a personal build gets you 90 percent of the daily loop. If you want to browse hundreds of curated spaces on your phone, pay them.
coreLoopDIY: A single fullscreen page that loops a background scene from your own list, plays ambient audio, runs a Pomodoro timer with session counts, and keeps a local to-do list, all persisted in the browser.
requirements: Your own scene sources: local video files or YouTube video/live IDs you are happy to embed
Ambient audio files or stream URLs you have rights to play
whatYouLose: A large curated library of scenes and licensed background music you did not have to source yourself
Native mobile and desktop apps, plus sync across devices
Co-working rooms and shared focus sessions with other people
Streaks, stats, and the light accountability layer built around them
Someone else keeping embeds and stream links from rotting
moatNotes: The scene and music library is licensed content, which is the one part of this you cannot cleanly clone. Everything around it is a timer.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because sourcing scenes is the actual work and nobody wants a second job curating loops of Tokyo in the rain. People also pay for the phone app, for the feeling of sitting in a room with strangers who are also working, and for not having to debug a dead embed at 9am when they were trying to start a deep work block. A local build is genuinely fine for one person with fixed habits and three favourite scenes; it is not fine if variety is the point.
notes: One of the rare cases where the DIY version can be better, because your five favourite scenes beat a library you scroll instead of working.
prompt:
Build a local-first "focus space" web app in an empty folder. Stack: Vite + React + TypeScript + Tailwind. No backend, no accounts, no analytics, no telemetry.

What it does:
- Fullscreen background scene, either a looping local mp4 (muted, autoplay, loop, object-cover) or an embedded YouTube video/live stream via iframe with autoplay and mute params.
- Scenes come from src/scenes.ts: an array of { id, name, type: 'video' | 'youtube', src, tags }. Seed it with 4 placeholder entries and a comment explaining exactly how to add local files in /public/scenes or a YouTube ID.
- Scene picker: a slide-in panel with a grid of scene names, filter by tag, click to switch. Remember the last scene in localStorage.
- Ambient audio: separate HTML audio element with its own volume slider, independent of scene video volume. Sources from src/sounds.ts: { id, name, src } supporting local files in /public/sounds or stream URLs. Include a simple mixer so more than one sound can play at once, each with its own volume.
- Pomodoro timer: configurable focus/short break/long break lengths, auto-advance toggle, big monospace countdown, start/pause/reset, session counter for the day. Timer state survives a page reload using localStorage plus a stored end timestamp so it stays accurate.
- To-do list: add, check off, delete, reorder by drag, persisted in localStorage. Optionally attach the active task name under the timer.
- Chrome-free by default: overlays fade out after 3 seconds of no mouse movement and fade back in on move. Keyboard shortcuts: space toggles timer, S opens scenes, M mutes all audio, F requests fullscreen.

Explicitly out of scope: user accounts, cloud sync, mobile apps, shared rooms, any bundled copyrighted video or music. Ship with empty media folders and README instructions for adding your own.

Deliver: working npm run dev, a README covering how to add scenes and sounds, and no .env needed since there are no secrets. Keep the whole thing under roughly 800 lines and do not add a state management library.
